utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wladimiroff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I'm grateful for your coming back. Thank you very much. General, would you be willing to make a list of the sources you reviewed when writing your report, or is this simply this: You saw the indictment and you saw the three binders of materials collected and selected by Mr. Coo and that's what you saw?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can give you, without further research, a list of documents which I have certainly had access to and read. And I think the main one I should draw your attention to is one which I think will be presented to the Court later, at a later period, which is the military analyst's report, which is an extensive document of some 600-odd pages, at a guess - I haven't got it in front of me. I have, of course, read the law on the army of Yugoslavia and the law on defence. I read the pre-trial brief and the rules for international law of armed conflicts, and of course, you'll see various references in my statement that have been directly pertinent to this particular portion of the Court's hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a question about page 3, if you would be so kind as to look at that page of your report.

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: In the first three paragraphs, you say: "This top level in the military chain of command..." and so on, adding, "commanding those operations in the field." Do you see that passage?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't got it. Could you give me a lead-in again, please? The first paragraph, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, starting with, "Thus, we see that the top level..."

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: And the whole paragraph itself.

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I take it that you here express the general principle of your deriving from your experience and this is not a finding of yourself based on what you know about the VJ; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That particular paragraph is referring, first of all, to general practice, and secondly, specifically to the VJ based on the information put in front of me. Whether it actually worked or not is -- I can't obviously say because I didn't have access there and I haven't interviewed anybody concerned with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. May I draw your attention to page 10.

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: And the first three paragraphs, starting with, "In Kosovo..."

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: There you make a reference to the FRY president, and I emphasise that part of that paragraph. Do you say this on the basis of the documents you have seen, that you say that all that you mentioned can be viewed as evidence that the FRY president wanted to maintain? Have you seen documents that make it utterly clear that this was his view, or is that your assumption?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you just give me a minute to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- refresh my memory reading it. Could you please just elaborate on the first part of your question where you say -- where you say -- you mentioned " ... can be viewed as evidence that the FRY president wanted to maintain?" Perhaps there was a couple of words not put on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: The question is: Were you able, on the basis of the documents that have been shown to you, to establish that what you say before: "In Kosovo, I understand that the Joint Command headed by a civilian (politician) was responsible for coordinating joint VJ-MUP operations. This, as I mentioned, can be viewed as evidence that the FRY President wanted to maintain..." and so on. Did you actually see materials that made it clear that the FRY president wanted that?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't answer that. I would have to -- I mean, I wrote this from the documents that were put in front of me and in good faith, and to give you an accurate, guaranteed accurate answer, I'd have to do further research. But what I would say is that, in more general terms, that it would be most unusual to have part of the army not under control of the Commander-in-Chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Right. If I draw your attention to page 13, where you write about special operations, I realise that you've got a lot of experience in your time dealing with special operations. I'm not going to question that. What I want to ask you is this: Did you have specific materials dealing with paramilitary working in the context of a military action? Not separate units acting separately from an army but within the context of an army.

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand the police are divided into -- or the MUP are divided into two sections, one of which is the civilian -- normal policing, civilian control, and the other is the more the state, extension of the state arm of the police and responsible for special operations and also for intelligence collection, perhaps arguably more of a counter-terrorist nature more than routine policing matters. My comments here were of a general nature in that I was expanding my initial more detailed -- in more detail my initial introduction into the need for coordination and control and how it would work, which is what I was called upon to do, put before the Court. And in that context, what I say there is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What I'm also referring to were the paramilitary units not being a part of the MUP or the army but working together with the army.

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you point out the specific part?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It's not in your report, so that's the reason I ask.

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see. I have had documents put in front of me explaining the construction of the -- the breakdown of control -- breakdown of organisation within the MUP up to a certain extent, and if that is what the MUP in Serbia were in fact practising - and there was no evidence to the contrary and indeed there was evidence to show that that was their normal -- their normal organisation, method of operating - then obviously they have a special forces area. But I think we want to -- I want to clarify this special operations, seeing, if I may, that you've raised the issue. I'm talking here of special operations, whether they are police or whether they are military or whether they're some third force.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what I'm saying is that you cannot have special operations so special that they go on -- take place in a military area without the military commander knowing that they are happening unless you're going to court fratricide and uncoordinated operations which will lead to, eventually, some form of disaster.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I understood. That was the reason why I asked whether you had anything in front of you dealing with the paramilitary who are not with the police, not a part of the police, not a part of the VJ because you do not mention anything about that in your report.

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just thinking a minute. I can't recall reading anything to suggest that there was a paramilitary organisation operating in Kosovo, from the information put in front of me, that did not either come from the police or from the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. If I may draw your attention to page 20, first paragraph, starting with, "I would agree ..." In that part of the paragraph, I emphasise again the President of Yugoslavia. You say: "I would agree with the conclusion that, based on the information such as that in the --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speaker please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I'm told to slow down, so I will. "I would agree with the conclusion that, based on information such as that in the preceding extract, the President of Yugoslavia has ultimate responsibility for the discipline and standards within the VJ." Is that a finding or was it totally based on materials you have seen or was it your assumption on the basis of what normal practice would be?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is based on the material that I have seen. It is not based on personal experience because I was not there. And on the material I've seen, it is stated quite clearly what the chain of command is, or should be, and if that was operating in Yugoslavia at this particular time, then clearly what I say in that paragraph is -- explains the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Actually, what you say now is, if I understand you well, that the President of Yugoslavia would ultimately be responsible for and so on.

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not clear of the significance you're trying to put on the change of wording. Which word are you suggesting you delete from my statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Well, here you said, "President of Yugoslavia has..."

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I suggest, if I understand you well, what you mean is the President of Yugoslavia would have ultimate responsibility for, and so on.

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I entirely accept that. If -- obviously, if that system had been abrogated, then whatever was put in its place, which I had no knowledge, would operate differently. But if it was a standard system the Yugoslav army was practising, that would be the state of affairs, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Right. If I may draw your attention, finally, to page 29, where we find a summary which one also may understand as a conclusion. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It may sound a silly question, but I take it that Queen Elizabeth, being head of state, is not the Commander-in-Chief of the British army, isn't she?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Who is the Commander-in-Chief within the UK?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Commander-in-Chief of the services in the UK is the chief of defence staff, reporting directly to the government and working alongside the Defence Minister who represents the Prime Minister, and as such, he has -- the CGS -- the CDS, chief of defence staff, has direct access to the Prime Minister himself at the chief of defence staff's request at any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Am I right in thinking, then, that your experience and your time does not encompass a Commander-in-Chief in your system in the sense as you refer to here?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, let me explain what I've already -- add a little to what I've already said in reply to the last question. That is that, in my view, if the British forces behaved in a manner that was unacceptable or which failed, I would expect the -- some of the responsibility of that to fall upon the Prime Minister's shoulders. Certainly a significant amount would fall on the chief of defence staff's shoulders as the Commander-in-Chief. Now, so far as my experience of working with a Commander-in-Chief and a head of state, let me be -- put this quite clearly and firmly. The army in any democratic country is not an independent body, independent of the government of the day, and whatever command structure may have been set up to work in that country, the army is a part of that structure, with its authority emanating from the most senior politician in the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: In your summary, you say, and I will read it to you --

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I hadn't quite finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Finish, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- collect my thoughts. You were a bit quick.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We must be quite clear that the army is the tool of the politicians. It is not an independent organisation running affairs as it sees fit. It is the tool of the politicians, an extension of politics. All military matters are. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before you continue, General, I did have some concerns about the conclusions that you have drawn in that paragraph, and I might as well express them now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It is the extent to which you extrapolate from a particular constitutional and legal system that it seems to me might not necessarily have been operating in Yugoslavia. For example, in answer to the question from the amicus just now, you spoke of the army in a democratic country not being an independent body, independent of the government of the day, and that whatever command structure may have been set up to work in that country, the army is part of that structure, with its authority emanating from the most senior politician in that country. Now, that may be true and is true of most modern armies in the Western world, but you seem to draw from that that the same system operated in Yugoslavia without presenting any concrete evidence that this is in fact so. And I might as well go further. Your entire set of conclusions, and as it is set out in the summary, is postulated, is it not, that on -- on the assumption that the Yugoslav army is a well-organised army, well-organised in the same way that the army in the United Kingdom or in Jamaica or the United States is organised and that, therefore, the passage of information from the upper echelons to the lower echelons, from the lower echelons to the upper echelons runs smoothly. But that assumption may not hold in a situation of conflict. Did you address that particular question, that that entire premise on which you worked of a well-organised, well-structured army may not have been functioning in the situation of conflict that Yugoslavia was functioning and how that would affect the conclusions that you have drawn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my summary is based on the assumptions that I have made throughout my evidence, which I don't think I need probably repeat, but the key assumption so far as your question is concerned is that the Yugoslav army was operating according to international law, according to the -- according to the law on the army in Yugoslavia and according to the chain of command that formerly existed in 1999. And if that is so, and it's not for me to say whether it was so or whether it wasn't, but if that is so - and I had to assume that it was so in my case - then what I have said is accurate. I haven't finished. If there was a breakdown in the passage of information and a breakdown of such magnitude that the central government didn't know what its army was doing and indeed the Commander-in-Chief didn't know what its army was doing and had no control over it, then clearly you had on your hands the next best thing to an insurrection going on in one part of Yugoslavia where the forces of the state were conducting themselves independently of the state's wishes and the head of state's wishes. I saw no evidence to suggest this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Wladimiroff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honours. Judge Robinson really touched on the matter in two questions I asked. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Picking up on those last points, first of all the point about a Commander-in-Chief, in your experience of countries presided over by presidents controlling the executive, is there any sensible parallel to be drawn between such presidents and a constitutional monarch like Queen Elizabeth of England?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Queen Elizabeth of England, to my mind, does not come into this discussion. Although she's the constitutional head of the country, the actual executive head is the Prime Minister. And I would have thought that there were plenty of parallels between the Prime Minister's position and the President of Yugoslavia's position on the evidence that I've had put in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You think -- specifically with His Honour Judge Robinson's most recent queries and concerns, is the detail of the chain of command as evidenced by documents dealt with in the report of Mr. Coo?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And as I explained earlier, typically we would have preferred your evidence to come after his but, for organisational reasons, that wasn't possible. I think you've dealt with this: Is there any evidence in fact shown to you going to show that this was not a well-organised and responsive army, responsive to the executive?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you were asked a question by Mr. Wladimiroff, if we'd like to be good enough, please, to come back to page 20 in your report to see that question in its full context. You have to come back to page 19. At the foot of page 19, if you'd be good enough, General. Amongst the material you were able to review was Article 136 of the very constitution under which the accused was operating, and it goes over the page and says this: "The President of the Republic shall appoint, promote, and dismiss from the service, Officers of the Army of Yugoslavia stipulated by Federal Law: shall appoint and dismiss the President, Judges," and so on. You then say: "I would agree with a conclusion that, based on information such as that in the preceding extract, the President of Yugoslavia has ultimate responsibility for the discipline and standards within the VJ." Is that at the root of your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no cause to change that comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That is the setting of this particular question by Mr. Wladimiroff where I think he wanted you to substitute the word "has" by the word "would be" and you were prevailed on to accept that. It was in the course of that question he used the term "Commander-in-Chief." Do you remember a question by the accused to you about control of the forces where he used the term "Commander-in-Chief" of himself. Do you remember that question?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Go back to one of the other questions that Mr. Wladimiroff --

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can I just re-emphasise this, if I may?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we go back to the top of page 20 again and that extract, my evidence is not based on what was actually happening on the ground, because I wasn't there. It was based on documentary evidence and the laws of the land that were put in front of me, and that extract is typical of the sort of evidence with which I was working. Now if the whole thing had been changed and they are working under a different premise and different structure, and a different organisation and different level of responsibility, then clearly what I've said would not be correct. But I think that extract in itself from the Article 136 of the constitution emphasises what the state should have been unless somebody had changed the rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And do you remember the questions asked by the accused in broad terms; there was no suggestion to you that the rules had been changed?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no indication that the rules had been changed, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would you be good enough to come back to one of Mr. Wladimiroff's earlier proposals. Page 10. "I understand that the Joint Command" - middle of the page - "headed by a civilian (politician) was responsible for coordinating joint VJ-MUP operations." Now, it may be or it may be not that you can remember where that particular detail come from. If you can't, don't trouble about it because we can dig it out from the sources we'll turn to in a second, but if there was a civilian politician responsible for coordinating joint MUP-VJ operations, does that sustain the following sentence, namely that this can be viewed as evidence of the executive wanting to maintain authority and control?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be evidence that the situation -- that the Yugoslavs were behaving according to the regulations that they themselves had set up and expected to work to, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You said early this morning, when Mr. Wladimiroff started to ask you about sources, that you were in a position to provide, I think, a list. Did you speak of a list or a schedule?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave all I've got in front of me. I can't, I'm afraid, say that that is totally comprehensive without leaving the room and doing further research. I read an immense amount of stuff. You know, I don't have a legal mind and absorb all this at the first go, I'd have to go and look at the documents, the actual documents I've read and list them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you still have in your papers - because if you do we can just put it on the overhead projector - the list of documents that was provided by Mr. Coo or others of my colleagues when you were asked to prepare this report? I think it came in certainly two batches but there was a list of documents provided. If you've got it in your papers. It may not be there. If not, I'll get Mr. Coo to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a list which I was working off which was in a private note to me, asking me to make sure that I re-read and read again the certain documents which I read out just now, and detailing particular paragraphs. But in fact I read all these documents that he's put in front of me, like the law of the army of Yugoslavia. I read through pages and pages of that, including the recommended paragraphs, and I just wonder whether it is right to put up a document that might not be complete and whether it wouldn't be better to produce something for the Court that is complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. And included in the material you read, did you read the pre-trial brief, do you recall, and Mr. Coo's report?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry, if you want to --

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nothing further to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll deal with the list of material available to the witness through Mr. Coo on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A couple of other questions arising from things asked of you by the accused. At one stage, if I followed his line of questioning correctly, he was postulating a well-organised army - because he never challenged that - he was postulating that a well-organised army under pressure because of the bombing by NATO. Do you remember that passage of questions?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I think inviting you to allow for the possibility that such an army might find excesses committed or errors made by soldiers because of the pressure they were under. Just supposing that happened, would that affect at all the duty of commanders at all levels to review actions and to take appropriate disciplinary steps after the immediate crisis was over?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it would not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you see any evidence or indication of disciplinary steps taken in respect of the humanitarian violations that on the basis of the indictment and only on that basis you assume to have happened?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand the word "disciplinary measures taken" at an exceedingly junior level. A few cases which I don't have before me. But there was a total lack of any investigatory evidence produced to me or indications of disciplinary measures being taken at any effective level of command, and this would imply either that people weren't doing their job or they chose not to conduct those investigations. And indeed the reverse is the case; many officers received acclaim for their role in the operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then finally, you were asked questions by the accused such as, "Can you imagine an officer ordering execution?" You remember he was sometimes asked to rephrase such questions, but the thrust of his questioning was that there could be no such thing as illegal or improper orders. If in fact - and it's entirely for the Judges to find - there were human rights violations or crimes committed by a well-organised army on a widespread basis, and you've told us that we have almost no orders to review because they haven't been produced, but if you have such a widespread pattern, whatever the organisation of the army, what does that say about orders that must have existed at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did actually say -- touch on this in my own response to that question, as earlier stated in the evidence. The extent of the excesses mentioned in the indictment were such that in no way could they have been the odd rogue commander, the odd rogue unit just going his own way and deciding to take the law into his own hands. They required a degree of logistic support to implement them, a degree of coordinated military operations to make them effective. That must have implied that the forces in Kosovo were receiving instructions to behave in this manner. We do not have any written directions suggesting what these instructions were and indeed nor are there -- nor is there any record of war diaries or situation reports. So one can only make the assumption that the instructions were given verbally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have no other questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Sir Peter, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. No, Mr. Milosevic. We've heard from you. The witness has concluded his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the videolink, there's one matter I'm going to deal with. Mr. Milosevic, your time for cross-examination is the time allotted. As you'll find when you call your witnesses, the other party then can't have another go because it feels like it after re-examination and after cross-examination unless there are exceptional circumstances. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the videolink is ready, Mr. Ryneveld will take the next witness who has, of course, facial distortion as well as a pseudonym. My own experience of the sometimes intermittent service of the videolink and problems means that we do have another witness in the building in reserve should that ever become necessary. And even if I'm not in the court for a couple of minutes, I'll always be able to be found and come back and deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, perhaps we can deal with the timing of this witness. There seems to be a substantial witness in terms of length, but do you anticipate being able to get through the evidence reasonably expeditiously?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That is my hope, yes, Your Honour. I would hope to be able to complete him within one full session, but I see that I've lost half a session now, so it would be probably the balance of this session and probably an hour into the next session. Looking at about an hour and a half to complete my examination-in-chief, depending, of course, on technological impediments preventing speed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Clearly there must be time for cross-examination. Do we have the videolink tomorrow, if it's necessary? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I have not been told that it is not available. The equipment is there, the witness is there; it ought be. However, I can inquire during the break in the event that is not the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm in the hands of the AV booth to let me know whether or not we are in fact hooked up to the videolink and, if so, which screen we are to use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The registry will deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Here we are. Thank you very much. I see the image on the Video Evidence button, however, I want to ensure before we start that it's only the Court that is able to see that image and there is distortion, in fact, to the public at large. I'm just apprehensive. Can we be assured that we have distortion? Yes. Two thumbs up means that we can go.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have facial distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let the witness take the declaration. Yes. Do we have the sound? Yes. Could the witness try again and take the declaration and see if we can hear it

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you'd like to sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have about three or four questions to ask in closed session and then the balance of the evidence ought be in open session. Might that be arranged now, please? So --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: --- Break taken at 9.47 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I gather the videolink can be available - although it will be administratively problematic - but it can be available tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next witness has facial distortion but is not concerned that his name should not be known. And in the summary that has been provided, and I hope in time for you to read, there is an explanation he gives about his attitude towards facial distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, your full name.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Zoran Stijovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Stijovic, at the application of the Prosecution, your evidence is only being broadcast with facial distortion. Is that because this was requested on behalf of your employers who insisted upon it, you yourself being entirely content to give evidence openly had your employers not taken the view they did?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Stijovic, are you an officer of the Republic of Serbia's security information agency, formerly known as the State Security Service or RDB, having been employed by the Ministry of Internal Affairs since 1990?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In April of last year, in the capacity of assistant head of the DB of Belgrade, were you appointed to interview General Radomir Markovic, former head of state security and a witness earlier in these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you interview him on several occasions, covering many topics?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I was officially appointed to carry out part of the official assignment related to Mr. Markovic while he was in detention in the district prison in Belgrade, and these interviews took place over a longer period of time; from the month of April until the month of July 2001. The topics were different, and this was a higher level of collecting information for the state security. On the basis of the facts that I obtained from him, we would later consult and then we would continue working with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, he was detained at the time, facing criminal process himself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Proceedings are still taking place in the District Court in Belgrade, and he is the accused party in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The particular investigation or interview in which this Chamber has an interest concerns the refrigerator truck. Was that interview part of the investigation into his own alleged crimes or was that in relation to some other more general inquiry?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: No. As for Mr. Markovic, I talked to him. I had interviews with him related to other topics. That is to say not pertaining to this particular topic. So I did not know anything about the refrigerator truck case except for what was made public in the media in that period. In that period, that was a very big thing in the media, if I can put it that way. So this topic simply imposed itself in this interview. That is to say, this refrigerator that was found in the Danube, and it was imposed primarily because in some of the writings in the media, notably the tabloids, there were particular speculations that surfaces, namely that the RDB was involved in this, namely our unit for special operations, that is to say, one of our elite units that is the constant target of attempts to discredit it. And that was the reason that led the leadership of my service to instruct me to discuss this topic with Mr. Markovic in prison, that he should tell me and explain to me the role of the State Security Service in that, whether there was any truth in this, whether any part of the RDB took part in this and possibly whether he knew anything about this case. That was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Under what part of your criminal procedure, if any, was this interview conducted?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: In our country, this is very clearly defined, that is to say work with detainees, persons who are in detention. Also, the authority of the interior is quite clearly defined. That is to say the rights and responsibilities of the agencies involved therein. That involves the State Security Service as well. So this is Article 151 paragraph (2) of the Law on Criminal Procedure that gives the right to persons involved in the agency of the interior to interview persons who are in detention and to collect information on certain things that may be of interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Of course, the Court here may not be familiar with the details of that criminal procedure and may not need to know more than a few details. First, this is not, I think, an investigation by an investigating judge but an investigation conducted by yourself; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: This is the so called pre-criminal procedure. And during these proceedings, the agencies of the Ministry of the Interior collect information. According to the principles of work involved in my service, we are supposed to verify this information and facts that are obtained. On the basis of a possible confirmation of these facts and this information, then one goes before an investigating judge. What is characteristic of this particular article of the law is that a statement or statements are taken. Please understand this term "statement" in the form of minutes, records that are taken from the interviewees. This cannot be used as evidence in a court of law.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Stijovic, thank you. We'll come to that in a second, and have regard to the interpreters and -- they haven't yet complained, but they may prefer you to speak a little more slowly because I think you're faster than me, and they usually complain about me. What rights, if any, does the person being interviewed have? Does he have to answer or is he entitled to maintain his silence?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: The person being interviewed by the members of the Ministry of the Interior, according to this Article of the law, enjoys significant rights. First of all, such a person can refuse an interview on this subject. So the authority given to the employees of the Ministry of the Interior actually hinges on the willingness of the person involved to discuss such matters at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And when being questioned, assuming he's been, in principle, willing to cooperate, is he entitled to decline to answer particular questions put by you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, at any point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where did these interviews take place?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Basically, I conducted these interviews completely in accordance with the Law on Criminal Procedure. That is to say that the interviews were conducted in official premises, that is to say separate premises of the district penitentiary in Belgrade. These are premises that are used for interviewees of investigators and investigative judges with persons who are in detention. They're also used by lawyers and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think you were accompanied on these interviews by another staff member. Can you just give us her name and then tell us what equipment she had with her and what part, if any, she took in taking the statement.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I conducted these interviews with Mrs. Olivera Antonic-Simic. She is a talented staff member from our agency. And in that particular case, that is to say these interviews that I had with Radomir Markovic, she was a technical staff member. She had a laptop and a printer with her, and in that room we talked and we documented the course of the interview between Markovic and myself. So she was a purely technical person. She recorded the statement, printed it, and signed it, eventually, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In general, before we look at this particular interview in which we have an interest, but in general, did the person being interviewed, Mr. Markovic, make any amendments or corrections to first drafts of the statement that were produced? Just explain the system without going into too much detail but enough to let us have a picture of it.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the interviewee, in this case Mr. Markovic, actively participated in drafting this document, this statement, that is. At any point in time, he could participate in that during the course of the interview. I just need to explain how this took place in brief terms, as you said. I put questions to Markovic. He answered. I took written notes during the interview, and when something interesting cropped up, in my assessment, then I would dictate that, in his presence, to Mrs. Olivera Antonic, and then she reported that on the laptop; and at any point in time, Mr. Markovic, as indeed was the case in some situations, reacted or could react. And sometimes he himself would dictate portions of the statement, portions of the interview that we were conducting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, at the end of the process, were final versions printed, hard copies, produced from Mrs. Antonic-Simic's laptop computer and printer?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the essence of the process was as follows: When the laptop part would finish, then Mrs. Olivera Antonic would print out one copy, a working draft I could call it, and then Mr. Markovic would take it, he would examine it in detail, and then he would amend it to a point. However, I have to say that these amendments were not of any substantive nature. Sometimes it was just questions of style, grammar, et cetera. Such amendments were then put into the statement by Olivera on the laptop and then we would print out that statement in the required number of copies. Then again Mr. Markovic would look at it, examine it, and once he would agree, then, according to customary procedure, he would sign the statement and put the date thereon. Then Olivera Antonic and I would do that finally. And before that, we would destroy, in his presence, the working draft.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I wonder if the Registry could produce Exhibit 283 and 283A. And if we could first of all lay on the overhead projector, so that people can see it, the pages of the B/C/S version, which is 283. There are three pages of it, and we'll just look at it fairly slowly. Page 1 to begin with. Mr. Stijovic, this exhibit, the exhibit with which we are concerned, does this reflect an interview -- was this the product of an interview that you had with Mr. Markovic on the 2nd of June of 2001? You can see it on the overhead projector -- or on the screen. The screen's not working. There it is. This is the first page of the exhibit, the three pages. Is this the product of an interview on the 2nd of June, 2001, between you and Mr. Markovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want to deal first with the format of the record so that those viewing who don't have hard copies themselves can understand it. It begins at the top with a declaration, and then that's signed. And whose is that signature that follows?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: This is the signature of Mr. Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The body of the statement starts. We see at the foot of the first page that there's a signature. Whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: That is also the signature of Mr. Markovic. And the date affixed there was affixed by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Going to the next sheet, please, sheet 2. First looking at the top of it, right at the top. And is it on the screen? I've got a video thing on the screen now. We see at the top of this page a signature, and we can probably already start to recognise it. If we can now go to the bottom of the page, we see a signature, again with a date. That's the signature of?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Of Radomir Markovic. And he also put the date on it below the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then on the third sheet, turn to that, please. At the top and on the bottom right-hand side, the same two signatures again; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again with the date. In the middle of the page, we see Olivera Antonic-Simic's name and signature. And on the left-hand side, what do we have there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: On the left-hand side is my own signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the title above your signature translates as -- can you just read out what it says there.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: This is the usual procedural format. The interviewee accepts in full consciousness that this document can be used in further proceedings before judicial authorities. That is to say that the person concerned is willing and ready to explain this with full responsibility and in detail if necessary. So then it should go to an investigating judge, and then an investigating judge should check all of this out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The two words and three abbreviations above your name, can you just read those out for us, please. "Izjavu Uzeo" and so on. Could you just read those out.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: "Statement taken by," and then it says, "Authorised officer," and then, "Zoran Stijovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we then take that version off the overhead projector, hand it to the witness. Place the English version, page 1, on the overhead projector, You will see the opening endorsement reads: "I, Radomir Markovic --" with date of birth and so on -- "make the following statement, being before an authorised officer of the MUP of Serbia state security department, Centre Belgrade, voluntarily pursuant to Article 151 subsection 2 of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia's Law on Criminal Procedure on the premises of the county prison, Belgrade, 2nd of June, 2001." Now, Mr. Stijovic, the body of the statement we are some degree familiar with, but if we look at it a little bit further down to remind ourselves, it deals with the refrigerator truck, and in the seventh line in the English version - it will be different in your version, and I think you do speak some English so follow whichever you prefer -- And, Your Honour, I should say this is still a draft translation. We've been pressing for a final version; it should be with us tomorrow. In I think the seventh line, it sets out: "Vlajko Stojiljkovic, as Minister of the Interior, Vlastimir Djordjevic, as the Public Security Department Head, and I attended the meeting. Most likely, the meeting was dedicated to the Kosovo issue and attended by, besides the above-mentioned people, VJ representatives although I cannot say that with absolute certainty." It may be an obvious question and answer from what you've told us, but where did detail like that come from? Did it come from you or did it come from Mr. Markovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think I said beforehand that as for the refrigerator truck, I did not know anything about it, I did not hear anything about it except for what I saw in the media. I said that in that period, this was hot news in the media, and police and other officials were referring to it as well. Except for that and the instruction to ask Mr. Markovic about this, I did not know anything about it. So what is stated here is a reflection of the facts actually stated by Mr. Markovic. I did not include anything else, and I did not change the course of what he said nor did I exert any pressure on him. What he said is what he said. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And we take it from that, just looking at the next two sentences, you needn't look for any more detail, that it was Vlastimir Djordjevic who raised the issue of the removal of Albanian corpses, and in the following sentence, it was Mr. Markovic saying that it was in that respect that Milosevic ordered Stojiljkovic to take necessary measures to remove the corpses of Albanian civilians that had already been buried. That all came from Mr. Markovic, I take it.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I told the investigators, I think yesterday, and I think I told you too yesterday that I understood this, that is to say I have been working with these cases where we had a lot of knowledge and information about manipulations with corpses. So I understood this just as a responsible task and assignment which the organs of public security were to perform and to stop any possible manipulation with it, or with them. So this was customary procedure, the usual kind of work done after fighting had taken place in the territory it has taken place in, and that's what Markovic said, and that's how I recorded it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've recorded here the words that Markovic used, haven't you? Sorry?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it was for you to hand on the product of this statement to the investigating judge, for him to take the matter further?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was my job, according to customary procedure and the principles of subordination, which hold true in my agency, it was my job to hand it over to the competent seniors, senior officials. And quite simply, I was quite amazed to see that this kind of statement was used in court. First of all because the subject matter and contents, the substance of the statement, the seriousness of the doubts expressed, and I think that it should have been used as a guideline for further work and verification of those data. I handed it over anyway. I had no feedback information or feedback orders coming down to me nor did I have any further conversations with Mr. Markovic on the subject, and that was that. We had our conversation, discussed the subject that was imposed, and that was it. We carried on working on other matters and this went on up until July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Markovic ever complain about the way this statement had been taken or about its content?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: No. Mr. Markovic never complained about the course of my interview with him. Our relationship, as far as it can be said in a situation of that kind, was highly proper, conducted in a very professional manner. We discussed the topics he wanted to discuss. And he's not somebody upon whom I could exert any form of pressure either or to wield any influence on him and to influence him in any way, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Any question of your putting words into his mouth or providing text for him to sign which he did so when it hadn't come from him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. That would be -- that wouldn't at all be serious. A man with so much experience and years of work in the crime service. I've only been working there two years. He's devoted his entire life to the service. He is a serious, professional man. So it is quite out of the question that I could have done anything like that and supplanted something that he didn't want.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. I shan't take you any more through the detail. I think you were asked yesterday what recollection you have, quite apart from looking at this statement, of anything that Mr. Markovic said at the time, that is any vital live recollection you have about what he said about these events. Do you have any recollection?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the statement was taken more than a year ago, so that's a long period of time. I learnt that I would come before this body on the 16th of August this year. That's when they called me up, the people from the Operative Group of Serbia, and handed me the invitation. It was a surprise to me when I was summoned and that it had to do with my conversation with Radomir Markovic and my work with him in detention. I can't remember any details which would illustrate whether he corrected or changed anything, but I do know that he had very negative things to say about the fact that anything like that could have ever happened. And on several occasions, he used negative words and terms to describe what he thought. He used -- he said that it was a morbid job, and he didn't know who could have delved into that kind of thing, that it was a hard job to do, but of course a job is a job and it had to be done. So the gentleman yesterday, the investigator, reminded me that it was in the context of that statement that we mentioned the Racak case and in the context of manipulations with corpses and mistakes made. Had the police remained in the village of Racak on that particular night and provided security for that location where the fighting went on --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you. You're moving beyond the question.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you recall Mr. Markovic saying anything about the prospect of the truck and the bodies being discovered?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to be quite frank. He said it was an idiotic and even psychiatric case. That is to say the very idea would be idiotic, that somebody could push a refrigerator truck into the Danube carrying corpses and think that this would not be discovered. In a short while, in five years, in ten years, that that was quite beyond all reason. And I tend to agree with him there. I think that it is quite unbelievable. I don't want to enter into whether it is correct or incorrect, true or false, but that's what I thought at the time and that's what I think now. I don't know. What can I say?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: These observations, the morbid observation and the observation about the truck being discovered were made in the course of the discussion. They don't find themselves reduced to the statement which is more particular matters of detail; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you wait there, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stijovic, from your statement, I can see that in the month of April 2001, you were the assistant head of state security for Belgrade. Tell me, please, who at the time was the head of the State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: The head of the service at the time was Mr. Goran Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Goran Petrovic. I see. Is that the man who, with Rade Markovic, was brought up before the District Court in Belgrade? We saw court documents to that effect.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I think so. I saw that in the press. I'm not quite sure, but all I can say is that I think it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And was it clearly visible that they brought for -- took out Rade Markovic outside the district penitentiary and that they offered him, that they blackmailed him and offered him a change of identity if he gave up his complaints and the charges brought against me?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say whether anybody in addition to me talked to Mr. Markovic. What he told me, what Mr. Markovic told me was that he had had talks with Mr. Mijatovic, Mr. Petrovic, and Mr. Mihajlovic. Now, I did not ask him as to the contents of those conversations nor did I want to know about it, although perhaps Mr. Markovic would have liked to tell me about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That was at the District Court in Belgrade, and at the time, this is what was established. Now, do you know that Markovic made a statement in the premises of the prison, of the penitentiary, also in front of two boards of the federal parliament, the parliamentary committee, in fact?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you both. Could you remember that this has got to be interpreted, Mr. Milosevic, and also Mr. Stijovic. You both speak the same language and it's inevitable that you're going normally to respond, but could you leave a pause between question and answer. And also, Mr. Milosevic, after the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. May. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there were two parliamentary committees, and it is front of those two committees that he explained that illegally and without permission from the Court, he was taken out by the Minister - this man Petrovic, not to enumerate all the others - and that he was blackmailed, and said that he was asked to charge me with anything whatsoever in order for them to forgive him or to annul or to withdraw - because they had nothing to forgive him for, amnesty him for because he was innocent and in prison for a year and a half - that they offered him a change of identity, money, et cetera. Were you acquainted with this? Did you know about this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I did not know this directly. All I did learn was indirectly, through the press and what was published from the parliamentary committee meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you read the minutes from the parliamentary committee, the two parliamentary committees, in fact?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the information media did publicise this, so, yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you read about the discussion that was held in court about the same topic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you, Mr. Stijovic, in order to be able to ascertain the positions from which you appear here in court. So tell me this: Your testimony here, is it designed to demonstrate that Rade Markovic lied when he testified before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That's not a matter for the witness. That's a matter for us as to what his evidence is designed to do and what we draw from it. It's not for the witness to say. His evidence is purely as to what happened. Of course, the inference to draw is indeed that Mr. Markovic lied, but that's not a matter for the witness. It's something you can address us on in due course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, Radomir Markovic testified here under the solemn declaration, on oath. So I don't see any other purpose of this catching at straws by the opposing party other than attempting to prevail upon the witness and to question the statements of a police official of a regime that knows full well what it's doing, what it's about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, all that is a matter of argument. As I say, the purpose of calling the witness is obviously to produce evidence that Mr. Markovic didn't tell us the truth. Now, we heard Mr. Markovic's evidence. We've now heard the witness's evidence. It will be for the Trial Chamber to decide where the truth lies. In due course, you can address us on it. It will be one of, no doubt, the submissions you make when the time comes. But as I've told you with witnesses before, you can't ask them what the purpose of their evidence is because it's nothing to do with them. All they can say is what happened. And you've heard this witness's account of how Mr. Markovic came to make this statement, and of course you can ask him questions about that, if you wish, but you can't ask him what the purpose of his evidence is. It's not for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Or, Mr. Milosevic, if you have evidence which can rebut this witness's evidence, then you may consider adducing it at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stijovic, tell me this: How many individuals in any way, I mean people linked to the criminal persecution of Rade Markovic, how many of them did you talk to, you personally? How many people did you personally talk to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could I ask the witness to repeat what he just said, please. The interpreter apologises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Stijovic, you are asked by the interpreter to repeat your answer again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I was saying, I conducted a criminal procedure and brought charges against Mr. Markovic and against several other individuals, former employees of the State Security Service. And this procedure ended by a sentence passed by the District Court in Belgrade. The Supreme Court of Serbia looked into the case once again, and I think it will be delving into it in September again. It will be brought before the District Court again. And under those circumstances, I talked to -- I can't tell you the exact number of people, but I think it was between five and ten individuals. They were all former leaders and functionaries of the state security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, what did this sentence and judgement have to do with? What was the judgement about? What did it refer to, the judgement you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a closed case brought before the District Court. I can tell you what appeared in public and what was stated in public. It was my task, in fact, which was linked to the abuse or, rather, the re-recording of 15 CDs, diskettes on which we had individuals who were being investigated by the State Security Service, and they are all high-ranking functionaries, political and otherwise. They range from Mr. Kostunica, Mr. Zoran Djindjic and some others. Fifteen of them, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was that what the press wrote about, that the proceedings and that they were accused of divulging state secrets? Was that the case in question?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, of these ten or so individuals that you talked to, did you discuss any other accusations which were brought to bear against Radomir Markovic, that Radomir Markovic was charged with?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't want to talk about that here. I didn't come here of my own free will, and it is my fault that the statement was placed before this Tribunal here. I talked to Mr. Radomir Markovic about his role and the role of his service in the bygone period and very serious topics were discussed. And he spoke at great length. He spoke a great deal about these topics, but I don't think I can go into the contents of those conversations here and now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stijovic, if there are matters which you consider to be confidential, then you need not, without an order from the Court, divulge them. The relevant matter with which we are concerned is the statement about the refrigerated lorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you happen to know -- did you or anybody else from the State Security Service also blackmail and exert pressure on the individuals you talked to for them to bring charges against General Markovic in order for him to make charges against me?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I can say with full responsibility before you and before this Tribunal that I never blackmailed anybody, nor did I bring pressure to bear or threaten anybody in any other way or ask then in any other way to tell me what -- something they didn't want to tell me. They did so voluntarily; what they told me, they told me of their own free will.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, is it true, Mr. Stijovic, that with General Branko Djuric, for example, the former head of the Secretariat of the Interior for Belgrade, that you personally had several interviews, several conversations, one of which lasted for as much as ten hours in order to bring pressure to bear against him to bring charges against Radomir Markovic and to force General Markovic to in turn bring charges against me and accuse me?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: That is not true. I don't want to say what Branko Djuric talked about and everything we discussed. I don't wish in any way to contribute to the already difficult position of Radomir Markovic. And Branko Djuric knows full well what he said himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that you held similar conversations with Milan Radonjic, the former head of the state security of the centre in Belgrade, discussing the same topic with the same goal in mind?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: No, that is not true. I just had contacts with him when he was detained. We know each other -- we've known each other for a long time but I took no statement from him. I had no conversation of this kind. It was just as colleagues that we talked for a while, and the way this was interpreted later on by people from his entourage, I don't wish to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that with three other people, three other individuals who were alleged witnesses in the criminal case brought against Radomir Markovic, that you had the same kinds of talks?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I've already told you that I talked to people who were involved in the procedure itself and whom in one way or another were included into the overall procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, you claim that you talked to General Markovic on several occasions in the period between April and July 2001; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why don't you say that you talked to him several times both in February and March of that same year? Am I right or not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: No, you're not right. That's not true, not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know how many of your colleagues - and I'm thinking about members of the State Security Service - talked to Radomir Markovic at the period when he was arrested up until the present day and always with the same goal and target in mind, to exert pressure and bring duress against him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I think I've already answered that question. I cannot confirm or deny whether anybody talked to Mr. Markovic about that particular topic. I did not myself and I do not know whether anybody else did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you, contrary to the statement made by General Markovic which he gave here in The Hague, claim that he was not taken out from the district penitentiary to some sort of house where he was offered everything he was offered in order to bring charges against me and accuse me and confirm the allegations made by this false indictment here? Can you claim that he was not taken out?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot claim that. I think I've already said, Mr. Milosevic, that I -- all I can say is what I read about in the press. That's all I knew. And also that Mr. Markovic himself told me that he was taken out. He was taken out by the individuals that I mentioned a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean the minister, the head of the State Security Service, et cetera; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I didn't offer him any benefits. I had no authorisation to do so, to make any offers of that kind to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, but they, of course, did, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I'm just a small official in that whole structure, small clerk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what about the -- to exert pressure on somebody, is that a crime? Is it considered a crime to exert pressure and bring -- place somebody in a position of duress?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think it is, somebody to commit perjury.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you're well aware that the head of state security at the time did that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you ought to ask them that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Exactly. Now, you've made this point, Mr. Milosevic. The witness has given his answer. There's no point going on about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 2 of your statement, you state that you pinpointed the topics you would discuss with Markovic and that you decided on these topics with your superiors. Were they Petrovic and Mihajlovic again?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: That is not my statement. This is the portion put forward by Mr. Markovic, what Mr. Markovic said. I merely conveyed the fact he presented during our conversation. That I had consultations is true and not with Minister Mihajlovic and Mr. Petrovic but the person who was operatively in charge of this type of cooperation and cooperation, and that was Mr. Zoran Mijatovic, the deputy head of the state security department at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me this, please; when talking to General Markovic, Mr. Stijovic, did you call upon his attorney, the attorney defending him, and was he attended by counsel on those occasions?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no. There was no need for that. And this is clearly regulated by the Articles involved. Mr. Markovic, if he did not wish to reply to these things I asked him, he had the right to remain silent, and that is a right enjoyed by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But when the attorney is present, the Defence attorney. If somebody does not wish to make any statements on any subject, he has the right to do so and there's no difference there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Article 151 paragraph 2 of the Law on Criminal Procedure provides for the rules to be respected by the security organs vis-a-vis the interviewee.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you yourself state that the statements obtained in this way cannot be used as a basis for passing judgement. That is what it says in your statement. You say so yourself.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, you talked about a pre-criminal procedure here whereas now you said it was an information talk, an interview. Now, can that be a pre-criminal procedure or not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that is indeed a pre-criminal procedure. That is to say, when the internal affairs organs collect and amass information on a certain subject and afterwards we assess whether there are sufficient elements to take the case further and to make it a full-fledged criminal case and criminal procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stijovic, and I'm thinking about your conversations with Markovic here, was anyone else present, any of your colleagues from the State Security Service who could bear out what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from Olivera Antonic-Simic, there was no one else. They were confidential, secret conversations, and that was one of the conditions posed by Mr. Markovic for having the interview at all. So nobody else attended except the three of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. As far as you know, and I think myself, that Olivera Antonic-Simic was a typist, in fact. She was not an authorised official of the Ministry of the Interior. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's right, although she's not a typist. She's an employee of the agency, and at that particular moment she was there in that capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So she was in the capacity of a typist, basically?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But in fact she was not an official employee of the Ministry of the Interior which would be held to the rules of procedure and rules of service in conducting an interview; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it common knowledge that that type of interview, the kind of interview and conversation that you unfoundedly, I would say, called a pre-criminal procedure was conducted according to the rules of your profession, must always be held in the presence of two --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. You just put that the witness was wrong when you say it was a pre-criminal procedure. Now, if you're going to suggest that, you must put it to the witness and give him the opportunity to answer. Are you going to suggest that he's wrong in so describing the interview?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. Let us omit these explanations as to whether this is pre-criminal proceedings or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let us move on then and ask a question

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to repeat the question in an abbreviated form so that it will be clear to you as well, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that such interviews, that is to say informative interviews, are carried out according to the rules of your service always in the presence of two authorised officials? Is that right or is that not right, Mr. Stijovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: It's not right. I believe that I am a serious and well-experienced operations officer, and I was in a position to conduct such interviews often, and it is not true. The service does have other specific methods for documenting such interviews, and I believe that it is Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 9693 to 9700. not serious to discuss this subject in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it is not correct, according to your rules, that two authorised officials should be present during an interview?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: No, it is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. Am I right if I say that such an interview can then be treated only as some kind of operative information and nothing else?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: You're not right. That is just an orientational guideline for our work, a guideline in terms of how we should work, how to check out the facts. And this is one of the key principles of our service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Since this is one of the key principles of your service, and also on the basis of what you wrote here and also on the basis of regulations, this statement does not have any procedural legal, material legal value before courts in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: It cannot be used as evidence before -- for reaching judgement in a court of law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And when you let General Markovic sign his statement, did you caution him that this statement would be used before any court of law, The Hague Tribunal, or any other court? Did you say that to him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Frankly speaking, I cannot remember now whether I did caution him or not.
