But I thought and I do think, because we talked from the month of April onwards, that he is sufficiently experienced, that he's a good lawyer, and that he knows more or less what this means. However, I must admit that I am really surprised -- I was surprised when I saw that this statement reached the court for consideration. I think that the substance of the statement and the topics tackled required a more in-depth investigation and operational work and further investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you have any knowledge -- I'm asking you this, I'm not trying to accuse you of this, but I'm just asking you: Do you have any knowledge as to whether your superiors, that is to say those above you, your superiors who also unlawfully extradited me to The Hague, did they know the purpose why you gave this paper to Markovic for him to sign? Do they know that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I really do not know that, and I really cannot give you a precise and accurate answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Stijovic, did you follow the evidence of Mr. Markovic here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was on official business. I was out of Belgrade. And I mentioned at the very outset that I first learned that I would appear before this institution on the 16th of August this year when the Operative Group of the Ministry of the Interior called me and informed me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Then I have to read out to you parts of the transcript from Markovic's testimony here that pertains to this alleged statement of his here. In response to the Prosecutor's question, in response Mr. Nice's question, he says -- I'm sorry that the transcript is only in English: [In English] "I said to the investigators of The Hague Tribunal what is true in this statement, and I pointed out to them more than once during our interview --"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. There's an interruption.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's 8725, if you want it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, page 8725, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] "... to them more than once during our interview that this is a liberal interpretation of the employee of the office who made this report." [Interpretation] Then he speaks about the talks he had with colleagues at the Ministry of the Interior, and then he says towards the end within that same response on that same page: [In English] "... and not I ever spoke about these corpses and the need to transport them out of Kosovo and treat it according to the proper criminal procedure and the law." [Interpretation] A short while ago, you also said, Mr. Stijovic, the procedure that is carried out after combat operations, these are clean-up operations.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, clean-up operation, mopping up. It's the same thing for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that was the term used, and I assume that you know what this procedure mean.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, on page 8767 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We're not going to go -- you're not going to get away with putting half of something to anybody. You've put of what Markovic said, and you must allow the witness to answer. Mr. Markovic said that what we have here, the exhibit, the statement, was a liberal interpretation of what he said, taking that to mean a free interpretation, that is, not an accurate representation of what was said. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not correct. I do not wish to interpret the reasons or the motives why Mr. Markovic said that. What is correct is what I said at the very beginning. That is to say, the statement is a reflection of the actually presented facts by Mr. Markovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stijovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is a reflection of the truly presented facts by Mr. Markovic. I did not add anything there, nothing that was not said, nor did I affect the course of this conversation nor did I exert any pressure to him on the actual content of what he was saying. At any point in time, Mr. Markovic could stop this. He could refuse to sign it. He could say that this was a lie, that that is not the way it was, that I did not understand him properly. I mean, I'm sorry that I've been brought into this position too, but what can I do?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe you on that, but that's what he said here. Mr. Stijovic, you explained that you dictated the statement, and you say that Markovic, as a professional of many years of service, as nobody is denying, he's a general and so on, and he bore in mind that this should be professional, that it should be at a certain level as befits such a person. I am going to quote to you now a sentence that was quoted awhile ago by Mr. Nice, so please give me an answer. I am quoting it in terms of one question. This is a sentence that comes from this statement that was presented here to Mr. Markovic and now to you, and he says that this is your free interpretation and you say it is not, although you say that you dictated it and not him, and this is how the sentence reads: "This is a meeting that most probably was devoted to the subject of Kosovo and which was most probably, in addition to the persons mentioned, attended by the representatives of the army of Yugoslavia, although I cannot state that with absolute certainty." What does this look like to you? A professional, not a top professional of that nature, but any professional from the service, that it was most probably devoted to Kosovo, that it was most probably attended by some representatives of the army but he does not know which ones, et cetera. What does this look like to you? Does it look like a serious formulation to you or a serious interpretation of anybody's responsible professional statement, as if it's some kind of a field, meadow where there are thousands of people, not a small group of people who are in a room --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Question, Mr. Milosevic. Question, not speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The question is: Isn't this a caricature of a serious statement rather than a serious statement, Mr. Stijovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know what to say to you. Maybe you are overestimating Mr. Markovic's importance, but that's what he said and that's what I convoyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Stijovic. Let's move on. On this page 8767 from the transcript, the testimony of General Markovic, there is my question: [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... was related to this matter. You said it was a liberal interpretation on their part. You said it was a liberal interpretation on their part, that you discussed the mopping up in an informal conversation with Ilic, that what was said was mostly gossip, gossip, and that nobody, Ilic or you included, ever talked about removing corpses from Kosovo. So could it be said that this statement is a fabrication by the same people who conducted these interviews?" [Interpretation} Here comes his answer: [In English] "I did not read that statement before I signed it, and it is not really in the format of the statement. It was a conversation, an interview, in which we were looking for a way out of the problems that were facing the Ministry of the Interior. After that, an official -- an official, officer of the State Security Service, drafted this paper." [Interpretation] I am pausing because I hear the interpretation. When it finishes, then I continue: [In English] "Then when it was presented to me by the office of the Prosecutor of The Hague Tribunal, I pointed out certain details which did not tally with the truth. And after that I gave my statement to the investigators of the OTP, which I assert is true and correct."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, the witness should have a chance to deal with this before we go any further. Mr. Stijovic, I'm going to ask you some questions arising from what the accused has put. First of all, Mr. Markovic asserted that he didn't read the statement before he signed it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Next, he asserted that he --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Judge May, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He next asserted it was a conversation, an interview, "in which we were looking for a way out of the problems that was facing the Ministry of the Interior."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that his interpretation of that is different. We talked specifically about circumstances and events that took place then. That is to say the writings in the press about this alleged truck that was allegedly found in the Danube. And my concrete instructions to discuss this subject with him as the former head of state security, whether there was anything in it, what he knew about this, that he should tell us about that. So what he said is what I recorded here, and I do not see anywhere here in this statement that Mr. Markovic said that the bodies were carried from Kosovo and transported to Serbia. Had he said that, I would have written it down. And rest assured that anything in relation to that subject that is of substance, that is important, I would have certainly recorded on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. The last line on this very same page and then I move on to the next page. My question: [In English] "Is it true that the mopping up or the cleaning up means a lawful procedure consisting of those elements which you mentioned in chief, that is, removal of mines and explosives, removal of chemicals, removal of dead bodies, taking care of the wounded, repairing infrastructure, service lines, et cetera, that is creating, restoring life back to normal after combat operation; is that correct?"

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I think -- I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was my question to him. And he says [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... clean-up means, what implies." [Interpretation] And my question. [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... anyone at that meeting mention clean-up also means removal of traces of crimes or any sort of cover-up? Did anyone say that crimes needed to be covered up?" [Interpretation] Answer: [In English] "No. Nobody talked about crimes or covering them up." [Interpretation] Question again: [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... Ministry of Interior. Did anyone speak about the need to transfer some bodies from Kosovo to Serbia proper? Not that I have." [Interpretation] These are some of the questions and answers. I'll have some more. Now, please, does this coincide with what you talked about?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: It does, Mr. Milosevic. However, the order of these questions put by you was quite different. So this question of clean-up is one that I was very familiar with as a person that lived in Kosovo and did hard work in Pristina. Indeed, I know what it is. It is a highly responsible task. Now, what does "clean-up" mean? You mentioned all of that in your question. However, I would like to change the word order. So this first set, this procedure involves a series of measures, hygienic sanitary measures, that is to say the removal of corpses, of persons and animals, everything that is on the ground; and then a set of measures that are taken from a sanitary technical point of view related to livestock, the spread of disease, and other measures that are taken in order to provide security in certain areas where there were mines, radiation, et cetera. So this first set of hygienic sanitary measures meant also establishing the sites where there were possibly corpses that had been buried. There was a war going on. All sorts of things happened. There were also personal showdowns, there were killings. There were criminal offences. And the duty of these teams that were involved in this, both from the police and from the military, was to establish where these sites were, to find these sites, to dig them up, to establish the cause of death of these persons, to identify the corpses, and then to hand them over to the families and have them buried. If there was a single reason, if there was a single element that could give rise to suspicion that a crime had been committed, then the procedure stipulated by law had to be enforced, and that was it. That was my understanding of it. That is how I understood Mr. Markovic, and it is in that context that we mentioned the Racak case. Well, Mr. Nice interrupted me already when I started discussing that, so I really don't want to go beyond the scope.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you also understood that he spoke about the clean-up of the terrain.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, had I understood it any differently, had I understood that he had said something different, then I would have written it down that way. That's how I understood it and that's how I wrote it down, that these instructions were for that purpose, not for any other purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But did you hear now his statement when I asked him whether anybody mentioned any kind of cover-up of the corpses, some kind of transport of corpses, covering them up, hiding them, that his answer was no. Didn't he say to -- did he say to you that I ordered these corpses to be hidden? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Let me check. I'm going to read this, if you agree. May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from the main topic of the subject, Vlastimir Djordjevic, towards the very end, brought up the problem of removing Albanian corpses in order to eliminate any civilian casualties that could be investigated by The Hague Tribunal. Milosevic instructed Vlajko Stojiljkovic to take the necessary measures in order to remove the corpses of the already-buried Albanian civilians. I understood Mr. Markovic then that this procedure was supposed to be conducted according to regulations fully, and if we were to withdraw from Kosovo, which indeed did happen, we didn't want anybody to exhume these bodies and then to present this as something unlawful that had been done by us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But he precisely says that this is your free interpretation, nobody spoke about any Hague Tribunal at that time. And "clean-up" did not mean cover-up. On the contrary, it meant the legal procedure of establishing the cause of death of certain persons, burying them, informing the families, et cetera. Everything that "clean-up" means. After all, there are military instructions on clean-up. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and that is why I'm saying this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I think we have been over this. He has recorded -- the witness, I should say, says that he recorded what was taken down. Now, three-quarters of an hour we thought would be sufficient, but we'll give you until the adjournment. That's another seven minutes. This is a very narrow topic on which the witness is giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, it is a narrow topic, but it is a clear attempt by this false Prosecution to blame --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. No comment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean, this is not worthy of a civilised conversation, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it sounds as though you have no more questions. Does the amicus have a question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon, Mr. May. I do have questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Ask it, but make sure it's relevant and not repetition.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All of them are relevant, Mr. May. All of them are relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Stijovic, why on every page of the statement that you claim Rade Markovic gave to you of his own free will there is the date the 1st of June, 2002?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I noticed that when they showed it to me now in Belgrade in the month of August. Believe me, it's his handwriting. Markovic can also confirm this. I don't know. It's probably a mistake. I really cannot explain it in any other way. There is no intention. It's his handwriting. He can speak about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you claim that no pressure was exerted upon him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: No. I claim that I did not exert any pressure on him. Whether any pressure was exerted on him or not I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please slow down for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, you are putting opposite requests before me; to be slow and to be fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Staying in isolation in the prison in Belgrade for a year and a half, an innocent man being in isolation for a year and a half without any evidence and proof against him --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether Mr. Markovic is innocent or guilty. I don't know that he's been in an isolation cell for that long. When I talked to him from April until July, he was in an isolation cell. As of July, I have had no information as to where Mr. Markovic has been and whether anybody -- if anybody has been talking to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Markovic spent over a year and a half in solitary confinement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know. If you say so, I believe you, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that Markovic did not object to a single thing that relates to your conversation or to the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: During the conversation, he never drew my attention to the actual course of the interview that was taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you really saying that General Markovic was or is in a position to place any objections in terms of interviews that are taking place without the presence of his defence attorney or the representatives of courts, judiciary organs, and he is in a position to make any kind of objections?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic was not forced to do anything or to say anything that he did not wish to talk about. There were things, there were matters on which he was quite decided, and I was informed that he did not wish to discuss them. But there were also many serious issues that he did discuss and that he did give information to the State Security Service on, but he did not wish through this way, through Article 151, paragraph 2, to state these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Just keep it as brief as possible. For how many interviews that you conducted with Mr. Markovic do you have permission from the judicial authorities, that is to say the presidents of the relevant courts in Belgrade before which proceedings are taking place against Mr. Markovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I state with full responsibility that I had approval in writing as well from Nebojsa Zivkovic, investigating judge, investigating judge of the District Court in Belgrade for every conversation I had with Mr. Markovic and he was in charge of the proceedings against Mr. Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You claim that confidentiality and secrecy were one of the conditions that Markovic had put in terms of these interviews that you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: You mean all the interviews we had?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Then that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then why did you - how should I put this? - in a rather deceitful way, did you take a statement that he did not give and then, apart from regulations, according to the instructions of your superiors, you gave this statement here? Is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, what it -- you are putting -- you are putting -- just a moment. Before you start putting that witnesses were deceitful, you need a ground for that. Serious allegations of that sort should not be made without a ground. What the witness can answer is this: Can you assist, Mr. Stijovic, as to how the statement came to The Hague Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how it reached The Hague Tribunal. It was certainly through no fault of my own nor did I ever think that the statements that were taken from Radomir Markovic were supposed to be the subject of a discussion before any court of law. I'm not only referring to The Hague Tribunal, I'm referring to the courts in my country.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know that Radomir Markovic here, under oath, stated that you, Mr. Stijovic -- he did not mention your name actually, but he said the authorised official of the State Security Service, that you gave him an already-typed-out statement and under these circumstances, under pressure, that is, and after a year and a half in solitary confinement, he had to sign this statement, so practically under duress?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: That is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think on this topic it might be helpful if the accused gave us the page reference so we can have the precise terms that he says were used.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've quoted this to you exactly. And, Mr. Nice, you have the entire transcript, and you can read it as many times as you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer. This allegation has been made. The witness should have the opportunity of dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not correct. Mr. Milosevic, I am not here of my own free will also, but I am here under oath as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly? Did somebody take away the rank of police general from Rade Markovic? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then why do you write in this statement that you did not address him as "General" but as "Mr. Markovic" because he's in prison, et cetera, et cetera? Even if he's in prison and under investigation, he's still a general, I assume. Of your service at that.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I behaved towards him as I would behave towards any person who was in detention. This is my professional attitude, and it was not different at all in respect of any other individual I ever talked to who was in detention. I don't see any reason why I would have to change this attitude towards Mr. Markovic, and he never complained about my attitude or that I did not call him "General."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who could he complain to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: He could complain to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, he could complain to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you have now had well beyond the time that we gave you for this limited matter. You can ask one more question. Yes, one more.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. One more. Since that's the time you're giving me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday I received a statement - in all fairness, in English only - of Mrs. or Ms. Olivera Antonic-Simic. That is the person who typed this. And towards the end of her -- the first page of her statement, it says: [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... specific because this is not an original document. It also appears to bear the signature of Mr. Markovic and Zoran Stijovic. The content of the statement is familiar to me. However, I am really not in a position to confirm that the contents of the statement that has been shown to me are what I typed on that particular day." [Interpretation] So, Mr. Stijovic, as you can see, even your own official, your own staff member says that she cannot confirm that the contents of the statement shown to her are exactly what she typed that day.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I do not understand on the basis of what you infer that she confirmed or denied the substance of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am not questioning that nor do I harbour any illusions that under the pressure of this puppet regime, this quisling regime in Belgrade, that she's been ordered to say whatever she's supposed to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is the way we waste time. What is put -- what he's put, Mr. Stijovic, is that Mrs. Simic says that she's not in a position to confirm that the contents of the statement are what she typed. Is there any comment that you can make about that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I cannot make any comments with regard to what she said. I have said what I said. The statement is a faithful presentation of what Mr. Markovic said, and that is the content of the statement. And the signatures on the statement are my own, Olivera's and Mr. Markovic's. However, what I do wish to say before this Court, and that is what I informed the colleagues from the Operations Group of the MUP and the gentleman who talked to me is the following: When Mr. Markovic appeared in court, while I was working with him, there were very serious threats and pressures directed at me personally that in this way or that way I should change my statement before this Court. There were some pressures that I should additionally charge Mr. Rade Markovic and also that I should deny the authenticity of this statement. I said this to the persons in the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia, that is to say this Operations Group. I said this to the investigators. I did not come here as a result of my own wish, my own free will, but through the decision of my government. And as a clerk who -- a civil servant who respects his own government, I said the truth and I said that everything that this statement contains.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, in view of this statement made by the witness, can I just put one question to him, or two?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who asked you? Who asked you? Who asked you to additionally charge General Markovic, who asked you to deny what you wrote here in this statement? So these are two contradictory pressures that are being brought to bear upon you. So who asked for one and who asked for the other?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether I can do that and whether this is proper for me to say. Is it all right for me to say something like this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, unless you feel it would put you in any sort of difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I didn't seek closed session, for our part, but it may be something that could be dealt with in closed session if the witness has any concerns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, I think the sensible course is for us to adjourn. We will pursue this matter in closed session. Mr. Milosevic, you can ask two or three questions on that. We will then hear from the amicus for cross-examination. Mr. Nice, what is it proposed we should do then?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the link to Banja Luka is operational, we can obviously return to K41. If not, I'm not really in a position to start with Mr. Coo, but there is a short witness who could be interposed. That's John Zdrilic, and it might be that we could take his evidence in chief for the balance of this morning, postponing cross-examination until such time as may be convenient. He's, after all, available in the building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Those are the three remaining witnesses you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now. Mr. Stijovic, we are going to adjourn now for a break for 20 minutes. Could you remember, please, during the adjournment don't speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I several questions to ask with respect to the laws, Yugoslav laws and rules and regulations which relate to statements of this kind, the kind of statement that we have before us in court here. You spoke about voluntariness. And I don't want to go back to that subject, but let me ask you this: Witness Rade Markovic was not in prison -- had he not been in prison, is it normal legal procedure for anybody who is to give a statement in an informative interview should be called first, summoned first, and if he does not come forward, then he is taken into custody, detained, and taken to prison? So that that is the procedure, that there is no voluntariness there; if somebody fails to turn up, that he can be arrested; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we could put it that way, yes, and say that it is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what I'm interested in now is the following: Is it true and correct that at the time when this statement was given, as you say, according to Yugoslav laws, never -- nobody ever have the right of legal representation vis-a-vis the police organs, that is to say that nobody could bring in an attorney to represent them and so have the statement controlled.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: According to the law on criminal procedure in force at the time, that was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And is that the reason why the law provides for the fact that statements of this kind cannot be used for court purposes of any kind?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I explained that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I'm interested in the following: What happens to those statements once they are taken? The document, is it sealed and put away from the court files?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The investigating judge places it in a special binder and it cannot be used as evidence in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What I'm interested next -- in next is the statement we're discussing today. You can see that the statement was made on the 2nd of June, 2001. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also right that, before you, this statement was signed by Radomir Markovic and then by you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Radomir Markovic, the recording clerk, and then me; in that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, why was he the only one to place the date of the 2nd of June, 2002, if in the title page it says the 2nd of June, 2001?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the evidence does not support the 2nd of June. The witness dealt with it quite clearly. It's also apparent on the face of the documents that the man Markovic writes his 1s in a particular way. Mr. Tapuskovic should recall the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's right. Mr. Markovic, it was gone into in his evidence. He dealt with it, yes. And he didn't say -- he confirmed it wasn't 2, as I recollect. So, Mr. Tapuskovic, the evidence, as the Prosecution point out, doesn't support that particular representation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, but I know that it is a rule and regulation that if you have in the title page one date, then nobody's ever required to place a date underneath their signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can certainly ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could he explain that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can certainly ask the witness that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, the standard practice in my service - and you can check this out in statements taken by employees of the State Security Service - that the interviewee, underneath his signature, places the date in his own handwriting of when he gave the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And do you have to do the same?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, one more point. You said that you had authorisation from the investigating judge for the visit. I know that, according to the law, when a criminal case is ongoing, nobody can go and visit the person in prison to talk to him about anything, not even a police officer. Now, did you have an authorisation from the investigating judge, and is it true that you were not able to enter the prison without a permit of this kind for -- to conduct an interview?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. So I was given a written authorisation by the investigating judge, Mr. Nebojsa Zivkovic, who was in charge of the investigation against Mr. Markovic for that crime, and I was just authorised to discuss other topics, other subjects. I was not authorised nor did -- could I talk to him about --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's not what I asked you, Witness. What I'm interested in is whether, in prison, do they have this authorisation for each of these conversations?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they do. They have it in their logbook. It was a closed conversation. The principle of communication was different. It has the number of the official ID card, my signature, and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm clear on that about these records, but in prisons, do permits and authorisations exist? Are they stored in prison?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I couldn't have entered prison without having that kind of written authorisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A few questions, Your Honour, yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Stijovic, you said that more investigation was required beyond this statement. At the time of the preparation of this statement from Mr. Markovic, did you know where the bodies concerned had been taken and either handed over to relations or reburied? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Could you be more specific, please? What was your specific question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the time of taking the statement -- not taking the statement but having the investigation in the course of which you took the statement from Mr. Markovic, you say, in answer to the accused, that further investigations were required. I'm asking you, at the time of this investigation, did you know where bodies that had been dug up had been taken, either to be reburied or handed over to their relations? Just yes or no, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: You mean this particular case or generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Generally for these bodies that were dug up and that were referred to by Mr. Markovic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And where do you say they were taken? Just so we can have account of this.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: What I know is, as I was the head of the analytical department in the Pristina centre at the time, that there were several cases of this type, and I recall the Slovenija village incident where, in a mass grave, some 30 corpses were found. Once the bodies had been dug up and the identification of the bodies was conducted, the bodies were -- bodily remains were handed over to the family members.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's quite a different matter from the bodies in the truck. Had your investigations revealed where the bodies in the truck were going? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is this the sort of topic that might have been the subject of further inquiry?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: The state security department did not deal with this kind of question. We did not conduct the investigation. I don't know who did, but I do know full well that had we done it, had we done -- conducted it, that question would have required more in-depth analysis and concrete work.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You speak of the use that could be made or the use that could not be made of the interview of the type given to you by Mr. Markovic. You set out in your statement that there's -- there are provisions under Article 84 of the law of criminal evidence whereby such statements may be used in certain circumstances; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. I can remember two cases in point. At the request of the accused. That is the first condition. And the second is if death occurs, if the accused were to die. So specific conditions under which that statement can be used in criminal proceedings, in a court case. Otherwise, they are set aside, as I said a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Couple more questions. As to the form of the statement - I think you've dealt with this already - it was suggested to you by Mr. -- by the accused that you dictated the statement. In fact, did some of the words come from you or did all of the words come from you? Did some of the words come from Mr. Markovic? Just help us again so that we know what your evidence is.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember exactly now how the event actually evolved, but the procedure was as follows: I would dictate out loud the contents. I would dictate it to Mrs. Olivera Antonic-Simic. Mr. Markovic was present and took an active part in this. And he would interrupt me if he considered that my formulations or the turn of phrase I used was not adequate, did not correspond to what he said. I don't know whether that happened in this particular statement, but that's what happened. He would go through the stylistic errors later on, he would make his corrections, and that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two more questions. You were asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Nice. When answering a similar question asked by Mr. Nice previously, you put it this way: You've been working only for two years there, while Mr. Markovic devoted his entire life to this service. Do you remember that? You've only been working there for two years. So I'd like to clarify the meaning of "two years."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. That was an error in the interpretation. I said that Mr. Markovic spent his whole time in the crime police and the public security service and that two years of his own career, not my career, were spent in the State Security Service at a top level function as head of the service. So what I meant to say was this referred to Mr. Markovic, that he was in the State Security Service for two years. So this was a mistake in the interpretation. I quite certainly didn't say that. In 1998, he was appointed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just turning to the statement of Olivera Antonic-Simic, I'm not sure if the totality of the relevant passage was put to you so I'm just going to read it to you very slowly again. She says she was shown a photocopy of a statement. She goes on to say: "I have examined the statement and confirm that the copy statement appears to bear my signature. I cannot be more specific because this is not an original document." Now, that's all that was said. Do you have any doubts yourself as to the fact that this statement that's been shown to you with the signatures on all pages is the statement prepared on that day in June in the way you've described?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I have no doubts, and I think I stated this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally, you were asked a question by the accused following questions where he had quoted fully from the transcript, this being a question where he did not do so. And the question can be found on page 58 at line 20. He suggested to you that Mr. Radomir Markovic had stated under oath that you, Mr. Stijovic -- the accused added he didn't say your name but identified you as the authorised official. He went on to suggest that you gave him an already-typed-out statement and under these circumstances, under pressure, that is, and after a year and a half in solitary confinement, he had to sign this statement, so practically under duress. And you said that wasn't true. The accused declined to identify the passage, saying that I knew where it all was. Your Honour, the passage can be found, I think, at page 8787. And just to assist you, Mr. Stijovic, what happened with

utterances.speaker: MR. MARKOVIC WAS THIS
utterances.text: The accused put to Mr. Markovic in a single sentence not anything about duress. He suggested to Mr. Markovic the statement, "It was brought to you written the way it stands; right?" to which Mr. Markovic just gave the answer, "Yes." Now, dealing with the way the accused raised the issue in detail as opposed to the way he's recalled it being given today, what do you say to the suggestion made to Mr. Markovic by the accused that you brought him the statement already written, effectively, in the way it is now. Any truth in that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: There is no truth in that. It would be quite irresponsible and not serious, both on my side and Mr. Markovic's side, if we had both made an error of this nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nothing else from this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Stijovic, before you were stopped by Mr. Nice, you apparently tried to speak something about the Racak incident. Since Mr. Markovic, Radomir Markovic, answered to the question of Mr. Nice and myself regarding Racak and did mention something, I would like to hear what you tried to say before. To remind you, you mentioned about the manipulation of corpses and some police remained in the village of Racak or something like that. Could you tell us more.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. The Racak case is a very serious case, and Racak is the subject of various interpretations, and some people represent the case as being a crime, others see it as a montage of manipulation rigged by Albanian propaganda and information media. What I can tell you and what I know as somebody that has been in this kind of business, we know a great deal about manipulations of this kind and the abuses that can arise. What I said was that on that particular day, in the area of Racak, there was a combat operation under way and that in that fighting, there were people who were killed on both sides. As it -- darkness began to fall, the police withdrew, and I said - that is in my conversation with Markovic - had the police remained in Racak at all cost, at the cost of having reinforcements, today Racak would not quite certainly be the subject of a discussion and deliberation at this court or anywhere else. We would have known exactly whether it was a crime or whether it was manipulation and something along those lines. So I indicated the error that took place, the mistake that was made on the part of the police, the decision to have the police withdraw. The police ought to have remained on the spot to secure the locality and wait for the following day, the following morning, to undertake an investigation, as prescribed by law, and then all of us would know today what -- where the real truth lies and what actually did happen. That is what I wanted to say on that subject if you have understood me, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That was your personal observation, but what was the response of Mr. Markovic at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he and I were making comments to that effect. He roughly -- roughly portrayed this as a bad mistake, a mistake in assessment and also a mistake that resulted in grave consequences for my country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He said earlier that he didn't receive any direct information about Racak and he did not have much knowledge about the casualty of the civilians or something like that. He didn't know something about the Racak incident more than that.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Who did not get what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic said in this court that he didn't receive any direct report regarding Racak. Is it right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: He certainly got a certain type of information as to what happened there. He was in such a high position of high responsibility that in the system of information -- in the procedure of information in my agency, it is impossible that he would not be made aware of the operation and everything that was taking place in Racak. Absolutely. This does not correspond to the truth. I don't know what were all the details he knew about that, but that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stijovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Stijovic, in answer to Judge Kwon, you just said that you know about manipulations of that kind. Would you like to elaborate on that? Are you in any way suggesting that there is a practice of manipulation in matters of that kind in that area?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: May I give a bit of an extensive answer to this question, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is the way it is. For a very long time, I have been dealing with this problem and this work that pertains to Kosovo and the relations between the Serb and Albanian people down there. One of the characteristics, perhaps one could put it that way, of the Albanian ethnic community is this propensity for -- for staging this kind of theatre. The Albanian community is a very closed-off community, linguistically and in other ways. They have certain archaic ways of behaviour too, the manipulative techniques that are highly developed now - and it so happens to be that this is in my line of work so I do know something about this - such a community can create major problems. I'm going to mention a few cases to you that were very clear and in this way they can reflect that situation. In 1989, we had a kind of phenomenon whereby many miners were closed in the mine in Stari Trg, and then they said that many of them went blind. And then in 1991, we had this monoethnic poisoning. In this sense, a story started going around quite clearly that some kind of spray had been used. Can you imagine this? And that only Albanians were poisoned by this spray. So this was a theatre play, and it was presented for the entire public. Then, Albanians, according to religion, are Muslims. We have a few situations in which their behaviour completely differs from the behaviour and the obligations that Muslims have. For example, this has to do with the status of funerals and the status of the deceased. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is a limit of time, I'm afraid, Mr. Stijovic. One more example, if you please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, one more and then I will conclude. We had a mass funeral of Muslims in coffins with candles, and that is quite contrary to Muslim customs and everything else. But this was an image that was supposed to be portrayed to the public. So that is this dual morality that I'm talking about. There is one story that is told to the Albanian community and then there is this other story that goes outside the Albanian community, for the wider community. So one story is told within the Albanian community, and due to this exclusiveness of language, a super-real image is portrayed. Whereas in the external world, the picture is distorted and is adjusted to the needs and interests of that community. I don't know whether I managed to explain this to you really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. That has been helpful, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic -- Have you finished re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we have really exhausted all these topics. What is it you wanted to ask?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I avail myself of the right to put questions only in relation to the new question that was put by Mr. Kwon, in order to clarify things lest there be any misunderstanding or confusion, because I understand the witness very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You may ask, but it must be limited to one or two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm saying that because I understand the witness well, but I'm afraid that perhaps the broader public may not understand him sufficiently well and there may be some confusion in the true meaning of what he said here and what is the truth. Actually, Mr. Stijovic, when you talk about manipulations and manipulations in relation to Racak, you are referring to manipulations by the KLA and William Walker. Is that what you mean, those manipulations? Or let me make the question even clearer: You said that the police made a mistake because, after the battle, which is not being challenged, they did not remain, a police detachment did not remain there to guard the site because then there would be no scope for manipulation. Then they could not bring in any kind of corpses, then they could not present what was later used as propaganda, as was the case in Merkale and the street of Vase Miskina, against Yugoslavia; is that right? The police remained --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness -- let the witness answer, Mr. Milosevic, instead of all these long questions. You're asked to clarify what you meant by "manipulation."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But first of all, you are able to tell us whether you are in a position that there was a manipulation or not, first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall be quite specific. I mentioned the case in Racak as one event. That is being used for various interpretations. I cannot and will not say that this is a manipulation of the Serb side, that it is a manipulation of the Albanian side, or somebody else. What I want to say is that had the police remained on the spot after the fighting, even at the cost of further casualties or further reinforcements, we would not be discussing Racak any more at all. Definitely. The next morning, in the presence of the verifiers and appropriate crime investigation services, there would have been an on-site investigation, and it would have been quite clear what this was all about, whether this was manipulation by the members of the Kosovo Liberation Army, as is being claimed from one side, or was this a crime that was carried out by the other side? So the point is, the core of the matter is that this would not have happened had the police not made the mistake of withdrawing. I believe that that is the core of the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Stijovic, for coming to give your evidence to the Tribunal. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While the court is being prepared for the departure of this witness, may I say that I understand the position is we may not be able to make contact with K41 today. Mr. Ryneveld is in a position to take the evidence of John Zdrilic in direct, in chief, if that's acceptable to the Chamber, and we can then use him as a person in the building, whenever it's necessary, to finish his evidence assuming it doesn't conclude today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One of Mr. Ryneveld's phrases to do with wrapping around. He seems to be the author of many of these expressions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We have a developing dictionary of which "wrapping around" is one, "bis'ing" is another, and indeed "demi-bis'ing" is a third. But never mind. Before we turn to that witness, can I just return to Olivera Antonic-Simic. I'm not sure how available she's going to be next week, and in light of the evidence already given, I'm not really sure that it's necessary to call her, especially since the challenge, once seen in context, placed by the accused on the statement quite clearly is a challenge built on the fact that she's simply saying she hadn't seen an original document. I'll think about it overnight, but I think, I suspect, that the very least I will do is, in the jurisdictional terms with which Your Honour is familiar, tender the witness in case it is thought to be of importance for the accused. That is probably not a concept he will immediately understand so I might ask the Chamber to explain it to him tomorrow when I've decided how available she is and what my position is. I must say, for my part, I'm not sure that she would otherwise be necessary. Your Honour, I think that's all I need to say before we get on with the next evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I must say my reaction -- I must say that my reaction would be that it may not strictly be necessary to bring a witness with these sort of travel problems and the like to cover what can only be a pretty peripheral issue in the light of what she's said about it. I don't think it's really going to take us much further.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I take it we're in open session. It may be convenient, while the blinds are being removed, to deal with the evidence of Mr. Curtis and to say briefly that we have reconsidered the question of allowing Mr. Curtis to be called. On the further request of the Prosecution, on the reasons advanced by counsel, namely that his evidence related to investigations and, I would add, having read the statement, of exhumations, the Trial Chamber is of the view that it has heard sufficient evidence on those issues and considers more unnecessary. The other area urged is that relating to the arrest of the accused. The Trial Chamber is of the view that that also is not one on which further evidence should be allowed. The legal issues relating to the arrest have already been litigated and settled, and there is, therefore, no point, in our view, in calling further evidence to reopen the issues. And also, I would add, a matter which is not strictly relevant as far as the indictment is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] There was the issue of the correspondence with Judge Arbour. That could always, of course, be dealt with by Mr. Zdrilic as a matter of fact. I don't know that the Chamber gave specific consideration to that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? May I object?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, then Mr. Milosevic. You were saying that there was a question of the correspondence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, perhaps you could consider, if you want to pursue that, how to put it before us.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Apologise. We can put it before you through the witness John Zdrilic quite conveniently. It's simply a documentation in our possession, and it probably is important. I'm grateful for that opportunity and for that ruling. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice distorted my assertion in respect of quoting the statement of witness Olivera Antonic-Simic. I did indeed read a sentence that has to do with her statement regarding the signature, and she observes that this document was not an original. However, the point is not in the signature. The point is in the next sentence that I highlighted, and the next sentence reads as follows: [In English] "The content of the statement is familiar to me, however, I am really not in a position to confirm that the contents of the statement that has been shown to me are what I typed on that particular day." [Interpretation] Therefore, it is not really important at all whether the original was shown to her or not in order for her to be able to ascertain whether that's her signature or not. She says that she cannot confirm that the contents shown to her are what she had actually typed. That's the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Secondly -- I have another objection. Zdrilic was not announced for today. In the list of witnesses that was given to me specifically --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let me interrupt you. I know. We won't call on you to cross-examine him today. We'll merely deal with his evidence in chief, as it's called, or his direct evidence, and you can have time to prepare any cross-examination. And let me deal with one other administrative matter which I have, and that is a motion to call a witness after the 13th of September. We will grant it, the most recent. It's an application, the 2nd of September. We will grant it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Obliged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, can we have the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which witness is this? I would like to write it down too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will have closed session for that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Zdrilic, do I understand correctly, sir, that your full name is John Martin Zdrilic and that you have worked as an investigator for the Office of the Prosecutor since the 28th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZDRILIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Prior to coming to work for the Office of the Prosecutor, sir, you were a detective in the New South Wales police service?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZDRILIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: In Australia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZDRILIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Ryneveld, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: In Australia. Thank you. Now, sir, upon your arrival here, have you been largely involved in the investigation concerning the matters presently before the Court?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZDRILIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And as such, sir, did you have particular responsibility for the investigations in the southern part of Kosovo, which would include the municipalities of Prizren, Suva Reka, and Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZDRILIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And have you also been involved in the ICTY exhumation project, specifically in the summers of 1999 and 2000?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZDRILIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, very, very briefly just to put your evidence into context, can you explain very, very briefly what occurred in Suva Reka as it touches upon the evidence that I'm going to be leading from you today?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZDRILIC
utterances.text: I was tasked to investigate an alleged mass murder which occurred within the township of Suva Reka primarily in a disused cafe. It was as a result of that investigation where a number of exhumations were carried out and that also relates to my evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. And as a result of your investigation, sir, did you, in addition to investigating the scene in Suva Reka, conduct an investigation into an area known as Korisa and Ljubizda? I'm not sure if I've pronounced that correctly.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZDRILIC
utterances.text: That's correct. It related to a mass grave located between the villages of Korisa and Ljubizda in the municipality of Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please provide the Kosovo atlas page 11, please, and put that on the ELMO. And Your Honours, can I just address your attention to page 11 at the intersection of O and 21 and 22. That would be 21 and a half. And we can perhaps show that. We don't have it on the screen yet. Sorry. I don't have it on the screen. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, Suva Reka is shown there, and these two villages you refer to, could you point those out for us, please?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZDRILIC
utterances.text: Ljubizda and Korisa. Is that what you're asking for?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZDRILIC
utterances.text: This here is the village of Korisa, and this is the village of Ljubizda. This area down here is actually the township of Prizren. The area we're referring to is between the two villages I've just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And that orange just at the edge of the page, is that in fact part of Prizren?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZDRILIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. All right. Now, sir, did you attend at that particular area and can you tell the Court what is found between those two villages?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZDRILIC
utterances.text: It's a vacant area, and what used to be contained there and the remnants of are an old VJ firing range. Upon attending that location in 1999, what was found was the remainders of a mass grave which was subsequently examined and exhumed by the British forensic team.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. And those bodies, et cetera, from that examination or exhumation were videotaped and photographed, and were there any bones and artefacts located as well, do you know?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZDRILIC
utterances.text: There was. There was there were some bodies and some human remains, artefacts and personal effects located at that scene. The British forensic team, working on behalf of the OTP, fully examined that scene; videotaped, photographed, and logged.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And from that process, sir, are you aware whether any of the, shall we say, remains found at that firing range were identified?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZDRILIC
utterances.text: To date none of the remains were identified although the artefacts that were located there, there were at least 11 artefacts that were identified by family members as belonging to alleged victims of the Suva Reka cafe incident, and those artefacts pertain to at least six persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, I'd like you to address your mind to during 2001. Are you familiar with a gravesite having been located near Batajnica about which we've heard evidence? And if so, do you have any knowledge as to what investigations or subsequent DNA analyses have been performed with respect to such a site?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZDRILIC
utterances.text: Throughout that year there was a number of mass graves located within Serbia and a number of those graves were located at a site called Batajnica, which is a suburb on the outskirts of Belgrade in Serbia, found within the special anti-terrorist facility called May 13th at Batajnica. The first of those mass graves was called Batajnica 1, and as a result of -- that mass grave which DNA comparisons were done through the Madrid Institute in Spain.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. And you are familiar of that a colleague of yours, Mr. Fulton, had provided this Court with a preliminary report performed by the Spanish DNA team; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZDRILIC
utterances.text: That's correct. The bone samples taken from the bodies and the human remains located at Batajnica 1 were transported to the institute in Madrid. DNA comparison was done with those bone samples and blood samples taken from living -- from living relatives as a result of that -- as a result of that DNA comparison. To date, there have been two reports provided to the OTP. The first of which, the preliminary report has been produced to this court through my colleague Investigator William Fulton, and the second report is the report that we have here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honours, I understand that the preliminary report referred to by the witness is in fact Exhibit 166 and it's found at tab 28 of the Suva Reka binder which was also referred to and introduced during the evidence of Dr. Baccard, you will recall, when I called the pathologist. And so that is what that reference is to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've indicated that there is now an additional report. Perhaps we could have that report distributed at this time. While it's being distributed, sir, are you aware that this is a Spanish report from the Ministry of Justice which appears to have -- do you remember approximately when that was received? It bears a date of the 4th of July, 2002. Do you know approximately when that was received?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZDRILIC
utterances.text: It was received by the OTP some two weeks later. I believe it was the 16th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: When you get a copy of that document once it's been made an exhibit, there is a fax date at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Might that document be given an exhibit number, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 313.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: May I address the court on this issue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It seems to the amici that it's most unlikely that the accused will be able to cross-examine this witness on this closed exhibit so it is a matter for consideration for the Court, perhaps, to allow this document to be marked, not admitted, unless it has been clarified whether the accused has any issue related to the document as such. If not, yes, it may be admitted; otherwise, it should be submitted, in the view of the amici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the document can be admitted. It's simply a report which speaks for itself. If there are issues arising from it, it would seem to me that the document can be challenged, if there's a real issue arising from it, and further evidence, if necessary, could be called. As you know, we admit widely hearsay here, particularly official reports. But it's a matter which could be considered.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I have no problem with that. I just wanted to draw the attention of the Court to that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: For the reasons I have given, this document will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you've heard the Court indicate that this document speaks for itself. I'm going to ask you if you would, however, provide some background as to what you are aware of that the people in Madrid had available to them in order to prepare this report. In other words, what did they receive and can you just basically explain what occurred?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZDRILIC
utterances.text: As I've outlined, the Madrid labs, based on information provided by the OTP and received from the Belgrade Forensic Institute, some 59 bone samples. These were samples taken from bodies or human remains recovered from the Batajnica 1 exhumation site. They also received a number of blood samples. These are blood samples taken from, and again based on information taken from the OTP, based on relatives of the believed victims of the Suva Reka cafe incident from 1999. They also were provided by us with some family charts showing the relationship of the victims or the alleged victims of the cafe massacre, and the -- showing the relationship between the victims of that incident. They were also provided with -- then taking that information, they then conducted a DNA analysis or DNA comparison between the bone samples and the bloodstains which they had received.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Now, do I understand correctly, sir, that these family charts, did you produce some family charts, showing the victims and their familial relationships?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZDRILIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Madam -- Mr. Usher, could you show these to the witness, please. There are some additional copies. Your Honours, I'm looking at the clock, and I will not be able to finish my examination-in-chief in the four minutes remaining. I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When you get to a convenient time. We should adjourn on time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I will. I just thought I would alert the Court that rather than try to rush it, I probably need ten minutes in total, and I can't do it in four.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, just for the record, I'm showing you some documents that have the title of Annexure JZ-1 and right through 4, and there appear to be some charts. They've also been given ERN numbers. Looking at Annexure JZ-1, you produced this document, did you, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZDRILIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And can you, just very briefly, outline to the Court what it is that -- let's just deal with JZ-1. What does this -- what do these boxes mean and what happened?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZDRILIC
utterances.text: What I've depicted here, as I said, is the relationship of the alleged victims of the Suva Reka incident, the cafe incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sorry. It may be of assistance if we could put that chart on the ELMO so that anybody following your evidence would also be able to see what it is we're talking about. That's good. Thank you. Go ahead, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZDRILIC
utterances.text: In JZ-1, what I've attempted to do in the annexure itself is depict this particular family group. The head of this family group are the husband and wife, Vesel and Sofia, and they're depicted at the top of the chart, as I indicate here. The number in the brackets, naturally, is their age at that time in 1999. Stemming down from that, from Vesel and Sofia, are their children, and in this case it is Hajdin, Besim, Fatmire, Bege and Dasurije. These are the children of Vesel and Sofia. The names coupled with those, of course, are their married partners. In the case of Mihrije and Mevlude, again the ages by there. As denoted in the legend, down here, all those names that are depicted or have a cross beside them are persons that are alleged victims of the Suva Reka incident or the cafe incident in 1999. The names that are highlighted, which I'm indicating now, being Vesel, Sofia, Fatmire, Besim, Genci and Graniti, are all persons who have now been -- whose remains have been identified as being located at the exhumation site of Batajnica 1 in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. So the shaded names that were highlighted are in fact names referred to in the report, the Madrid report that we just had entered as an exhibit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZDRILIC
utterances.text: That's correct. The -- the addition of Genci and Graniti were in fact identified by DNA comparisons in the preliminary report received from Madrid, and then the additional four names and those two individuals as well were mentioned in the second report.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: My last question before the break, because we are instructed to stop on time: To your understanding, sir, the mitochondrial procedure that's referred to in the report, that goes through the maternal line -- the identification is made through the maternal line of the family; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZDRILIC
utterances.text: That's correct; "mitochondrial ligna" to my understanding, is the paternal and maternal matching through DNA comparisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I think the time has been reached, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we will adjourn now. We won't mark this as an exhibit. We will keep it there. We will deal with it in due course. Mr. Zdrilic, I should tell you, of course, not to speak, please, to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and will you be back tomorrow to conclude it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We will adjourn until tomorrow, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 6th day of September, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.
